questions.text: Which one of the following dependencies among the register operands of different instructions can cause a data hazard in a pipelined processor?
questions.solution:
A data hazard occurs when an instruction depends on the result of a nearby instruction that has not yet completed in the pipeline.

- Read-after-Write (RAW): a later instruction tries to read a register before an earlier instruction has written its new value — this is a true/flow dependency, and causes a genuine data hazard in a pipeline.
- Write-after-Read (WAR) and Write-after-Write (WAW) are anti-/output-dependencies; they cause hazards only in pipelines that allow out-of-order completion, not in a simple in-order pipeline.
- Read-after-Read is not a dependency at all — reads never conflict with each other.

Answer: Read-after-write

questions.text:
Consider the following recurrence relations:
For all [latex]n>1[/latex],

[latex] \begin{array}{l} T_{1}(n)=4 T_{1}\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+T_{2}(n) \\ T_{2}(n)=5 T_{2}\left(\frac{n}{4}\right)+\Theta\left(\log _{2} n\right) \end{array} [/latex]

Assume that for all [latex]n \leq 1, T_{1}(n)=1[/latex] and [latex]T_{2}(n)=1[/latex].
Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.solution:
First solve [latex]T_2(n)=5T_2(n/4)+\Theta(\log_2 n)[/latex].
Here [latex]a=5,\,b=4[/latex], so [latex]n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_4 5}[/latex]. Since [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n^{\log_4 5}[/latex] (as [latex]\log_4 5\approx1.16>0[/latex]), by the Master theorem (Case 1):
[latex]T_2(n)=\Theta\left(n^{\log_4 5}\right)[/latex].

Now solve [latex]T_1(n)=4T_1(n/2)+T_2(n)[/latex].
Here [latex]a=4,\,b=2[/latex], so [latex]n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_2 4}=n^2[/latex]. The extra term [latex]f(n)=T_2(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_4 5})=\Theta(n^{1.16\ldots})[/latex], which is polynomially smaller than [latex]n^2[/latex] (since [latex]n^2/n^{1.16}=n^{0.84}\to\infty[/latex]).
By Master theorem Case 1: [latex]T_1(n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]T_1(n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex]

questions.text: With respect to a TCP connection between a client and a server, which one of the following statements is true?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement about a TCP connection:

- TCP uses a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), not a two-way handshake — false.
- Either side (client or server) is free to initiate connection termination first; the server is not required to wait for the client — false.
- TCP is a full-duplex protocol — data can flow in both directions simultaneously — so "half-duplex" is false.
- TCP supports simultaneous close: both client and server can send a FIN at (roughly) the same time, and each independently acknowledges the other's FIN. This is a valid connection-termination scenario in TCP's state machine.

Answer: The client and server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time

The client and server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are true with respect to the interaction of a web browser with a web server using HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex]?
questions.solution:
HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections and pipelining over a single TCP connection:

- True: Multiple objects of the same webpage, if hosted on the same server, can be fetched over one persistent TCP connection — this is exactly the point of persistent connections.
- False: A single TCP connection is between one client and one specific server; objects stored on a different server require a separate TCP connection to that server. So this statement is false.
- True: HTTP/1.1 supports pipelining — a client can send a new request before the response to a previous request has been fully received, over the same connection.
- True: Since the TCP connection persists (is not closed after one request/response), multiple different webpages/resources from the same server can be downloaded over that same single connection, one after another.

Answer: Statements 1, 3, and 4 are true (same-server multi-object download, pipelining, multiple pages over one connection); statement about different servers over the same connection is false.

Click here for detail solution
options: HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple objects of the same webpage over the same TCP connection, if the objects are stored in the same server
HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple objects of the same webpage over the same TCP connection, even if they are stored in different servers
HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates sending a request for downloading one object without waiting for a previously requested object to be downloaded completely
HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple webpages on the same server to be downloaded over a single TCP connection

questions.text:
Let [latex]n>1[/latex]. Consider an [latex]n \times n[/latex] matrix [latex]M[/latex] with its elements from [latex]\mathbb{R}[/latex]. Let the vector [latex](0,1,0,0, \ldots, 0) \in \mathbb{R}^{n}[/latex] be in the null space of [latex]M[/latex].
Which of the following options is/are always correct?
questions.solution:
Since [latex](0,1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex] is in the null space of [latex]M[/latex], we have [latex]M\cdot(0,1,0,\ldots,0)^T=\mathbf{0}[/latex]. But [latex]M[/latex] times this unit vector simply extracts the 2nd column of [latex]M[/latex]. So the 2nd column of [latex]M[/latex] is entirely zero.

- Determinant: A matrix with an all-zero column always has determinant [latex]0[/latex]. So "[latex]\det(M)=0[/latex]" is always true. ("[latex]\det(M)=1[/latex]" is always false.)
- Rank: The rank could be anywhere from [latex]0[/latex] to [latex]n-1[/latex] depending on the other columns, so "rank [latex]=1[/latex]" is not always true.
- Null space size: Since the null space contains the nonzero vector [latex](0,1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], it also contains every scalar multiple of it (e.g. [latex](0,2,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], [latex](0,-1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], etc.), giving infinitely many, hence at least two, distinct non-zero vectors in the null space. This is always true.

Answer: Determinant of M is 0; and there are at least two non-zero vectors in the null space of M.
